sections.heading: Diagrams are marks: what examiners require on the page
paragraphs: Economics is a diagram subject and most students draw badly for a simple reason: nobody ever marked their diagrams line by line. A diagram in an Economics answer is not an illustration of the argument. It is part of the argument, and it carries its own marks, which are awarded for things that are mechanical and learnable. Axes labelled with the correct variables. Curves labelled. Original and new equilibrium both marked. The direction of a shift shown. Relevant areas identified and, where welfare is in question, shaded and named.

The habit that costs the most marks is drawing the diagram and then writing an argument that never refers to it. An examiner reading a correct diagram and a paragraph that does not mention any point on it cannot award the explanation marks that the diagram was supposed to support. The fix is a sentence pattern the student uses every time: state what shifts, state why it shifts, name the movement from the first labelled point to the second, and state the effect on price and quantity using the labels on the page.

Different parts of the course carry different diagram risks. Market diagrams suffer from carelessness. Externality diagrams suffer from unshaded welfare loss. Tariff diagrams have several distinct areas and students conflate them. Aggregate demand and supply diagrams suffer from inconsistent axis labelling, with students writing price rather than the general price level and output rather than real output. Each of those is a two-minute correction that is worth a mark every time it appears in an examination.

Practising this online is straightforward and arguably better than on paper, because a shared drawing surface lets the tutor build the diagram with the student, erase one label and ask what breaks, and save the finished version into a file the student revises from. A folder of the student's own correctly labelled diagrams, built over a term, is a better revision resource than any published set.
bullets: Label both axes with the exact variables the syllabus uses

sections.heading: The portfolio: three commentaries, and the rules that cost marks
paragraphs: The internally assessed portfolio is three commentaries of up to 800 words each, written on published news articles, and it is the only part of the Economics grade a student controls completely. It is also where marks are lost for reasons that have nothing to do with economics. The rules are administrative: three different units of the course, three different published sources, three different key concepts, and articles recent enough to satisfy the recency requirement at the time each commentary is written. A student who writes two commentaries on macroeconomics has capped the portfolio before a single piece of analysis is read.

Within those rules, the marks go to analysis rather than to summary. A weak commentary paraphrases the article and adds a diagram. A strong one takes one narrow economic question raised by the article, applies the relevant model with a labelled diagram, evaluates the analysis honestly within the word limit, and uses the key concept as a lens rather than as a label dropped into the introduction. Eight hundred words is short, which means the single most valuable editorial skill is cutting the article summary down to two or three sentences.

Article choice is where a week gets wasted. A piece that reports an event without any economic mechanism to analyse cannot be rescued by good writing. The test to apply before starting is whether the article lets the student draw a specific diagram and explain a specific causal chain. An article about a tariff, a subsidy, a price control, a central bank decision or an exchange rate movement usually passes that test. An article about a company's results usually does not, because it leads to business analysis rather than economics.

Support here is bounded, and the boundary should be in writing. A tutor may teach the economics, explain the rubric and its criteria, say whether an article permits analysis, and give feedback on the student's own draft in the way the school's own teacher does. A tutor may not choose the articles, supply paragraphs, rewrite the student's prose or produce a model commentary to be adapted. The student's own work is what is being assessed, and anything else is a malpractice exposure for the student rather than for whoever sold the service.

sections.heading: Command terms and the evaluation ladder
paragraphs: Every Economics question is built on a command term, and the term tells the candidate which level of response is being paid for. Define, list, calculate and state sit at the bottom and ask for recall or arithmetic with no development. Explain, analyse, suggest and distinguish sit in the middle and require a mechanism: something causes something, which causes something else. Evaluate, discuss, examine, justify and to what extent sit at the top and require a judgement supported by the analysis already given.

The characteristic failure at Higher Level is treating a top-level term as a middle-level one. A student asked to evaluate monetary policy writes a thorough explanation of how interest rates affect aggregate demand and stops. The economics is correct and the answer is capped, because nothing has been weighed and nothing has been decided. Evaluation marks need the conditions under which the policy works, the conditions under which it does not, some reference to magnitude or time lag, and a conclusion that commits.

A reliable structure helps more than any list of connectives. For an evaluation question: define the terms being used, explain the mechanism with a labelled diagram, give the strongest argument on the other side with its own mechanism, identify what the answer depends on, and conclude by saying which way the balance falls and why. Students resist concluding because committing feels risky. In mark-scheme terms, refusing to commit is the risk.

Definitions deserve a separate word. Short definition questions are the most reliable marks on Paper 2, and they are frequently lost to vagueness. A definition should name the category the term belongs to and the feature that distinguishes it, in one sentence, using the syllabus wording where the syllabus has wording. Students who learn thirty definitions precisely, in the course's own language, pick up marks on every paper for a few hours of work.
bullets: Define, calculate and state ask for no development at all

sections.heading: What the market charges, and the hour an Ajman family gets back
paragraphs: Families searching for an Economics tutor in Ajman usually begin by picturing someone at the dining table. That market is real and it has a price. Published UAE rate sources, including Bestimate's 2026 tutoring cost tables, put in-home one-to-one tuition at roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour with travel priced in, qualified online subject tutors at roughly AED 150 to 300, examination-level specialists at roughly AED 200 to 450 or more, and a premium named tier above that. Budget providers advertise from well below those bands. Those are market figures from published sources, not IB Gram prices.

For Higher Level Economics the supply question matters more than the rate. A tutor who can teach the policy paper, mark a Paper 2 evaluation against the published scheme and advise on portfolio article choice is a narrow specialism. Within a short drive of Al Mowaihat or Al Jurf there are few such people, and they are already committed in the weeks before mocks. A family restricted to a driving radius is not selecting the best available Higher Level Economics specialist; it is selecting the best one nearby, and paying a travel premium for the privilege.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE. Home tutoring is offered only in India, and every UAE lesson is one-to-one over live video. For a diagram subject that is a genuine advantage rather than a concession: the diagram is built on a shared surface, labels can be removed to test understanding, and the finished version is saved into the student's own folder. The scheduling gain is plainer still. For a household where a parent returns from Dubai at 19:00, the lesson starts when the student is ready rather than when a tutor has crossed two emirates.

The honest limitations are worth saying. Online needs a stable connection, somewhere the student can draw, and ninety undisturbed minutes. Where a household cannot provide those, online delivery works less well, and the free trial lesson is the moment to find that out rather than week five of a paid arrangement.

sections.heading: Permits, regulators and the questions to ask before paying
paragraphs: Private tutoring in the UAE is a permitted activity with conditions, not an unregulated one, and the position is clearer than most tutoring websites suggest. Individuals giving private lessons need a private tutor work permit from the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation, introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. The permit is granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include teachers registered at government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged fifteen to eighteen. Applications are made through the MoHRE website, smart app and e-services system.

Two things follow for a parent. The first is that a tutor charging for lessons should be able to say whether they hold the permit, and anyone operating without one is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No fine schedule is published, so a specific figure quoted at you is not a verified figure. The second is that a tutoring business with premises and staff is a different legal object from an individual tutor, requiring an educational services permit from the relevant emirate authority. No tutoring platform should describe itself as approved by a regulator unless it holds the specific permit and can show the number.

School regulation is separate and emirate by emirate. Ajman's private schools sit under the federal Ministry of Education, alongside those in Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah. Dubai's answer to KHDA, Abu Dhabi's and Al Ain's to ADEK, Sharjah's to the Sharjah Private Education Authority, and Ras Al Khaimah's to its Department of Knowledge. Sharjah's and Ras Al Khaimah's authorities approve curricula, fees and assessment methods as well as inspecting, which is worth knowing for an Ajman family whose child crosses the border to school each day.

One further rule matters where a family is considering the child's own teacher. Abu Dhabi's regulator has professional-ethics rules barring school staff from paid private tutoring of students at their own school, and the MoHRE permit code of conduct addresses the same conflict. Ajman schools answer to the federal ministry, so the school's own policy and the permit conditions are what apply; ask the school in writing before any arrangement, because the awkwardness of asking afterwards is considerably greater.

process.title: Send a marked Paper 2
process.description: A data-response script with a teacher's marks on it is the most informative document in the subject. It shows whether definitions are precise, whether the extracts were used as evidence, whether diagrams carry labels, and whether the long evaluation reached a judgement. Send it before any conversation.

process.title: Free trial lesson with one marked question
process.description: One lesson at no cost and no card details, ending with a timed question marked against the published scheme. For Economics, ask specifically for a diagram to be marked line by line. That is the fastest available test of whether the tutor knows what an examiner credits.

process.title: Decide which of the three jobs you are buying
process.description: Content and diagrams, the Paper 3 quantitative block, or portfolio process coaching. These need different hours and different sequencing. A single open-ended weekly arrangement tends to drift into whatever the student mentions first and leaves the policy paper untouched.

process.title: Set the slot and the portfolio calendar
process.description: A fixed Gulf Standard Time slot that works for an Ajman evening, plus the school's own internal commentary deadlines written down. The portfolio deadlines are set inside the school and are visible months ahead, which makes them the easiest part of the year to plan around.

process.title: Review against the mark record
process.description: After six weeks, compare equivalent questions from the start and from the most recent session. Economics scores move visibly when diagram and evaluation technique improves. If the record is flat and the marking is genuinely happening, change the arrangement rather than extending it.

whyPoints.title: The policy paper taken seriously
whyPoints.description: Paper 3 is the component weekly lessons most often neglect, and it carries a large share of the Higher Level grade. Sessions on it are timed from the first minute, because the paper's difficulty is pace and format rather than conceptual depth.

whyPoints.title: Diagrams marked line by line
whyPoints.description: Axis labels, curve labels, both equilibria, shift direction and shaded welfare areas each carry marks. Work comes back with those marked individually rather than with a tick on the figure, so the student can see where the mark actually sat.

whyPoints.title: Portfolio help that stays inside the rules
whyPoints.description: Article suitability, rubric requirements, unit and key-concept spread, word count and source dates, all checked. The student chooses the articles and writes every word, with written feedback on their own document so the school can see the sequence.

whyPoints.title: Specialists rather than proximity
whyPoints.description: Online delivery means an Ajman family chooses from tutors who teach Higher Level Economics, not from those who live within a short drive of Al Rawda. For a subject with a Higher Level only paper, that distinction decides the quality of the hour.

whyPoints.title: Market rates quoted, not invented
whyPoints.description: The AED bands on this page come from published UAE rate sources with the year attached and are presented as the market, not as our price list. Where the honest answer is fewer paid hours and more timed past papers, that is what you will be told.

whyPoints.title: Scheduling that matches a northern emirates evening
whyPoints.description: Later weekday starts for households commuting to Dubai or Sharjah, weekend mornings during mock and portfolio windows, and post-iftar slots through Ramadan instead of a month's pause in the period that matters most.

faqs.question: What is Paper 3 in IB Economics and do Standard Level students sit it?
faqs.answer: Paper 3 is the policy paper and only Higher Level candidates sit it. It lasts an hour and three quarters, contains compulsory questions, and mixes calculation with explanation and a policy recommendation drawn from the quantitative content reserved for Higher Level: multipliers, elasticity arithmetic, tariff and welfare areas, Lorenz curves and Gini coefficients, balance-of-payments figures and terms of trade. It carries a substantial share of the Higher Level grade. Because it is the only component involving arithmetic, it is the one most often under-practised, and it is usually the fastest place to recover marks for a student writing well but scoring poorly.

faqs.question: Why does my son write good Economics essays and still get a 4 at Higher Level?
faqs.answer: Almost always because the marks are not where he is putting the effort. A Higher Level answer earns credit for defined terms, a fully labelled diagram referred to inside the prose, a causal chain, and an evaluation that commits to a judgement. Elegant discursive writing without those features is unrewardable. Look at his last marked script: if diagrams are absent or unlabelled, if the extracts are never quoted on Paper 2, or if long answers describe rather than decide, that is the diagnosis. Each of those is technique rather than knowledge, and technique moves faster than content.

faqs.question: How are the Economics commentaries structured and how long can each one be?
faqs.answer: The portfolio is three commentaries, each up to 800 words, written on published news articles. Each must draw on a different unit of the course, use a different published source, and be built around a different key concept, with articles recent enough to meet the recency requirement when written. Marks reward analysis rather than summary: one narrow economic question, the relevant model with a labelled diagram, honest evaluation inside the word limit. The administrative rules cause more lost marks than the economics does, so the spread across units, sources and concepts should be planned before the first commentary is started.

faqs.question: Which key concepts does IB Economics use and do they appear in the exams?
faqs.answer: The course is built on nine key concepts: scarcity, choice, efficiency, equity, economic well-being, sustainability, change, interdependence and intervention. They are not a separate topic to revise; they are lenses the course uses to connect content, and each portfolio commentary must be built around a different one. In the written papers they shape how questions are framed rather than being examined by name, so the practical value for a student is as a planning tool: asking which concept a question is really about often reveals the evaluation line the mark scheme is looking for.

faqs.question: My daughter keeps losing marks on Economics diagrams. What is she doing wrong?
faqs.answer: Usually one of four things. Axes labelled loosely, so price and output appear where the general price level and real output are required. Curves or equilibria unlabelled, so the examiner cannot see what moved. A shift drawn with no stated cause. Or the diagram drawn correctly and then never mentioned in the written answer, which forfeits the explanation marks it was meant to support. Ask for one diagram to be marked line by line in a trial lesson. Students usually fix all four habits within a fortnight once they see the marks separated out.

faqs.question: What does evaluate actually require in an Economics answer?
faqs.answer: A judgement, supported by analysis already given. The marks need the conditions under which the policy or effect holds, the conditions under which it does not, some consideration of magnitude or time lag, and a conclusion that states which way the balance falls and why. A thorough explanation with no weighing is the commonest capped answer at Higher Level. Students resist committing because it feels risky; in mark-scheme terms the refusal to commit is the risk. A structure that always ends with a stated decision adds marks across every paper that carries an evaluation question.

faqs.question: How many Economics sessions does a Higher Level student in Ajman usually need?
faqs.answer: It depends which of three jobs you are buying. Content and diagram work tends to run as a weekly slot across a term or more, following the school's own sequence. The Paper 3 quantitative block is short and intensive, commonly six to eight timed and properly marked papers, which is often the highest-return purchase for a student already writing well. Portfolio coaching is a handful of sessions timed to the school's internal commentary deadlines. Many Ajman families start weekly, add the Paper 3 block before mocks, and schedule portfolio sessions separately.

faqs.question: Can a tutor choose my child's Economics commentary articles?
faqs.answer: No, and a tutor who offers to is creating a problem for the student rather than solving one. The portfolio is internally assessed work that must be the student's own, which includes the selection of the articles and every word of the writing. What a tutor may legitimately do is teach the relevant economics, explain what the rubric requires, say whether a chosen article actually permits economic analysis before a week is spent on it, and give feedback on the student's own draft as the school's teacher would. Keep version history on the document so the drafting sequence is visible.

faqs.question: Is Higher Level Economics or Higher Level Business Management the better choice?
faqs.answer: They assess different things and suit different students. Economics is a modelling subject: diagrams, mechanisms, quantitative policy analysis, and a Higher Level paper requiring calculation. Business Management is applied and case-based, built around a pre-released case study and tools applied to real organisations. A student who enjoys abstraction and is comfortable with arithmetic usually does better in Economics; a student who reasons well about organisations and people often does better in Business Management. Check the entry requirements of the degrees under consideration on each university's own admissions pages, because some economics programmes specify subjects explicitly.

faqs.question: Does Higher Level Economics require Higher Level mathematics as well?
faqs.answer: Not for the Economics course itself. The Higher Level quantitative content is arithmetic and interpretation rather than advanced mathematics, and a competent Standard Level mathematics student can handle all of it with practice. University entry is a separate question: a number of economics degrees specify a mathematics requirement, and some specify which mathematics route they expect. That should be read on each university's own admissions page rather than taken from any tutoring site, because the requirements differ between institutions and between countries and they change between admission cycles.

faqs.question: Do Ajman students sit Economics exams in May or November?
faqs.answer: Schools in the UAE run the northern hemisphere timetable and their Diploma candidates sit the May series. The precise examination window, the registration deadlines and the results dates should be taken from your school's Diploma coordinator or from ibo.org, because secondary sources circulate inconsistent windows and internal deadlines differ between schools. What is stable and plannable is the shape of the run-in: portfolio commentaries spread across the course, mocks in the new year, then a window where only timed papers and targeted repair produce any gain.

faqs.question: Can Economics lessons move to later timings during Ramadan in Ajman?
faqs.answer: Yes, and moving them is better than pausing. School hours shorten during Ramadan and household evenings restructure around iftar, so a 17:00 slot becomes unworkable for many families while a 21:30 one becomes straightforward. Because Ramadan falls inside the Diploma year, a student who stops for a month loses part of the window where timed-paper practice matters most. Ask for the shifted slot in advance rather than in the first week, because late-evening hours across the northern emirates are the first to fill and a preferred tutor may not have one left.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send an Economics tutor to an address in Ajman?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; home tutoring is a service offered only in India. All UAE lessons are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. For Economics that arrangement helps rather than hinders, because diagrams are built on a shared drawing surface, labels can be removed to test understanding, and every finished diagram is saved into a folder the student revises from. The scheduling gain matters too: the session starts when the student is home rather than when a tutor has crossed Ajman or the Sharjah border.

faqs.question: What does the UAE private tutor permit cost and who can get one?
faqs.answer: It is granted free of charge and runs for two years. The permit was introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and is issued through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation. Eligible applicants include teachers registered at government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged fifteen to eighteen. Applications go through the MoHRE website, smart app and e-services system. Anyone tutoring without a permit is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule is published, so treat specific figures sceptically.

faqs.question: Will a Higher Level Economics grade help with UAE university equivalency?
faqs.answer: Equivalency is a Ministry of Education process assessed against published requirements per curriculum, and it is not something a tutoring platform performs or can accelerate. The British-track rules are published clearly: five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than grade E or 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from that count, plus one A-Level at grade E or two AS-Levels. For the IB, no points threshold should be taken from a tutoring page; verify it on moe.gov.ae or directly with the attestation authority. Tutoring is not a requirement of the process.

ajman/ib-dp-economics-hl-tutor.closingHeading: Bring a marked Paper 2 and a Paper 3 attempt
ajman/ib-dp-economics-hl-tutor.closingBody: Those two documents answer the question a conversation cannot. A marked data-response script shows whether definitions are precise, whether the extracts were used as evidence, whether diagrams carry their labels and whether long answers reach a judgement. A Paper 3 attempt shows whether the arithmetic has been practised at all. Send them, take the free trial lesson, and ask for one diagram and one evaluation question to be marked line by line. Lessons run one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, timed for an Ajman evening, with later starts for families commuting from Dubai or Sharjah and post-iftar slots through Ramadan.

ajman/ib-dp-english-a-language-and-liter.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach group one English at Diploma level: guided analysis of unseen non-literary texts, the comparative essay, the Individual Oral, and the Higher Level essay. Each profile names the levels taken and the text types the tutor is strongest on, which is the detail worth checking before the free first lesson.

intro.heading: Why a strong reader can score a 4 in English A Language and Literature
paragraphs: This is the subject in which parents are most often blindsided, and the reason is structural rather than mysterious. Language and Literature is not a course about appreciating books. Half of it is about non-literary text types — advertisements, speeches, opinion columns, photographs, graphic novels, infographics, political cartoons — and every assessment in it is marked against the same four criteria: understanding and interpretation, analysis and evaluation, focus and organisation, and language. A fluent writer who never addresses criterion B will keep landing in the middle band, however elegant the prose.

The components are worth knowing precisely, because each one fails differently. Standard Level sits Paper 1, a guided analysis of one unseen non-literary text, at 35 per cent; Paper 2, a comparative essay on two literary works, at 35 per cent; and the Individual Oral at 30 per cent. Higher Level sits Paper 1 with two unseen texts at 35 per cent, Paper 2 at 25, the Higher Level essay at 20, and the Individual Oral at 20. Confirm those weightings against the copy of the subject guide your child's school holds before planning around them.

Where the marks actually leave is consistent across the students we see from this emirate. Paper 1 goes wrong because candidates summarise a text rather than explain how it works on a reader. Paper 2 goes wrong because the comparison is abandoned halfway down the page. The Individual Oral goes wrong because the global issue is too broad to be argued in ten minutes. The Higher Level essay goes wrong because a line of inquiry was never a question. None of those are failures of English; they are failures of format, and format is teachable.

Ajman adds a practical complication. Group one English is taught everywhere, so supply is less of a problem here than in the sciences — but a Diploma English department in a school of this size is often one or two teachers, which means one marking voice and no second reader. A student who has only ever been marked by the person who taught them has no way of knowing whether a 13 out of 20 is generous or harsh. That second reading is the specific service most families in Al Nuaimiya, Al Rawda and Al Mowaihat are actually buying.

The sections below work through each component in the order the marks sit, name the non-literary text types that get skipped, and translate the criterion language that decides a band. There is also a plain answer to the question every parent asks about this subject: what can one hour a week realistically fix, and what cannot be fixed by tutoring at all. Lessons for Ajman students run one-to-one over live video, in Gulf Standard Time, with everything marked inside the document the student keeps.

ajman/ib-dp-english-a-language-and-liter.programmesIntro: Group one English runs through every IB programme, and the step into Diploma Language and Literature is the one that catches families out. Below is what each stage actually builds, and what it leaves missing, because the gap at the point of entry decides what the first term of tuition should address.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Middle Years language and literature is marked on criteria A to D — analysing, organising, producing text, and using language — which is genuinely close to the Diploma criteria in spirit. What it does not build is stamina for a guided analysis of an unseen text under time, or the habit of writing about a photograph or a speech with the same rigour as about a novel.
programmes.countryNote: Ajman's Middle Years cohort is concentrated at Ajman Academy, with alternatives a commute away in Sharjah. Families here ask us at option time whether a strong Middle Years English student will find Diploma Language and Literature comfortable. The useful test is a single unseen non-literary text with a guiding question; the result is usually a surprise and it saves a term of misplaced confidence.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: The course is organised around three areas of exploration — readers, writers and texts; time and space; and intertextuality — and seven central concepts including identity, culture, creativity, communication, transformation, perspective and representation. Standard Level studies four literary works and two non-literary bodies of work; Higher Level studies six literary works and three non-literary bodies of work.
programmes.countryNote: Diploma candidates are the audience for this page and almost all sit the May session. For an Ajman household the sequencing problem is specific: the Individual Oral recording window and the Higher Level essay deadline usually fall in the same term as the Extended Essay interim deadline. We book oral rehearsal and essay supervision as separate dated hours rather than folding them into a weekly subject slot.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: Where a school offers the Career-related Programme, candidates take Diploma courses alongside a career-related study and a compulsory language development component. Students taking group one English within it sit the same papers and the same oral, so every point on this page applies without adjustment. The reflective project replaces the Extended Essay.
programmes.countryNote: Career-related places in the northern emirates are limited, and Ajman families enquiring usually have an A-Level or BTEC route in Sharjah in mind as the alternative. We teach the English course identically. The scheduling benefit is real: reflective-project weeks do not collide with the Diploma core deadlines, which leaves January free for oral rehearsal.

programmes.name: Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS
programmes.description: An English Extended Essay is a natural choice for a strong group one student and a trap for a careless one, because a 4,000-word essay needs a question narrow enough to answer with close reading rather than a topic broad enough to describe. Theory of Knowledge overlaps usefully with the course's work on perspective and representation.
programmes.countryNote: The practical core issue for Ajman families is evening arithmetic. A household running a daily commute into Sharjah or Dubai has perhaps five usable weekday evenings a week, and in the second winter term the oral, the Higher Level essay and the Extended Essay all want the same ones. We quote core support separately so a family can see which deadline they are funding.

ajman/ib-dp-english-a-language-and-liter.subjectsIntro: A Language and Literature plan is built against components and text types, not against the course as a whole. Below are the assessed components, the areas of exploration, and the non-literary categories students most often reach the examination without having practised. Work out which two are losing marks before agreeing to anything weekly.

subjects.name: Paper 1: guided textual analysis
subjects.levels: SL one text; HL two texts
subjects.description: An unseen non-literary text with a guiding question, analysed under time. Standard Level analyses one; Higher Level analyses two. Marked out of 20 per analysis against criteria A to D at five marks each. The loss is almost always the same: description of content where the question asked how the text positions a reader.

subjects.name: Paper 2: the comparative essay
subjects.description: One essay from a choice of general questions, comparing two literary works studied during the course, written without the texts available. Thirty marks, with knowledge and interpretation and then analysis and evaluation each carrying ten. Comparison must be sustained to the final paragraph, which is where most candidates quietly give up.

subjects.name: The Individual Oral
subjects.description: Fifteen minutes: a ten-minute presentation on a global issue using one literary and one non-literary extract of no more than forty lines each, then five minutes of questions. Forty marks across four criteria at ten each. The commonest failure is a global issue so broad that neither extract can be examined closely.

subjects.name: The Higher Level essay
subjects.description: A formal essay of 1,200 to 1,500 words on one literary work or one non-literary body of work studied, developed from the learner portfolio and written to a line of inquiry the student frames. Twenty marks across criteria A to D at five each. A line of inquiry that is a topic rather than a question caps the grade before a word is written.

subjects.name: The learner portfolio
subjects.description: A mandatory record of the student's engagement with every text studied. It is never marked, which is why it is neglected, and the Higher Level essay is required to grow out of it. A thin portfolio in the first year is the single best predictor of a rushed and weak essay in the second.

subjects.name: Non-literary text types
subjects.levels: SL two bodies of work; HL three
subjects.description: Advertisements, speeches, opinion columns, photographs, infographics, political cartoons, blogs, travel writing and graphic novels. Half of what the course assesses and a fraction of what most students revise. Each type has its own conventions, and Paper 1 rewards naming them accurately rather than noticing them vaguely.

subjects.name: Area of exploration: readers, writers and texts
subjects.description: How meaning is constructed and how a reader's own position shapes it. The area where criterion B marks are won, because it supplies the vocabulary for talking about effect rather than content. Students who can discuss implied audience and authorial choice score here without needing more reading.

subjects.name: Area of exploration: time and space
subjects.description: How context of production and context of reception shape a text's meaning. The source of most Paper 2 comparison material, and the area where a student in the Gulf reading a nineteenth-century English novel has something genuinely interesting to say about reception, if anybody has taught them that it counts.

subjects.name: Area of exploration: intertextuality
subjects.description: Connecting texts: conventions, genre, and how works speak to each other. It underpins the comparative essay and the Individual Oral's pairing of a literary and a non-literary extract. Usually taught last and examined first, which is why it is the most common gap in a second-year student's preparation.

Students we support attend the schools below. The service families here most often want is an independent read of a Paper 2 essay or an Individual Oral rehearsal, judged against the criteria rather than against a classmate.

sections.heading: The components, their weightings, and which ones get practised
paragraphs: Before anybody is paid, write down the four components and their weightings, because families routinely spend on the wrong one. Standard Level has three assessments: the guided analysis paper at 35 per cent, the comparative essay at 35, and the Individual Oral at 30. Higher Level has four: the guided analysis paper at 35, the comparative essay at 25, the Higher Level essay at 20, and the Individual Oral at 20. Check these against your school's copy of the guide, because a plan built on a superseded outline wastes paid time.

Now compare that with what gets practised in a typical school year. Literary works are read, discussed and essayed, so Paper 2 material accumulates naturally. The Individual Oral gets a flurry of attention in the weeks before the recording. The Higher Level essay gets a deadline. Unseen non-literary analysis, which is the largest single block of marks at both levels, is often practised a handful of times, usually against the same two or three text types.

That mismatch is the reason most group one grades sit below where the student's reading would suggest. It is also the cheapest thing on this page to fix, because unseen analysis responds to volume and honest marking rather than to more content. A student who writes one timed analysis a week for a term, marked against the criteria rather than praised, will move. The table below sets each component against where its marks go missing, so a family can aim their hours rather than spread them.

sections.heading: Non-literary texts: half the course, a fraction of the revision
paragraphs: Standard Level students study two non-literary bodies of work and Higher Level students study three, and the unseen paper is drawn entirely from this half of the course. Yet when we ask a new student which text types they have analysed under time, the answer is usually an advertisement and an opinion column. That leaves speeches, photographs, infographics, political cartoons, travel writing, blogs and graphic novels as material they will meet for the first time in an examination.

Each type carries its own conventions and its own analytical vocabulary, and the examiner rewards naming them accurately. A photograph has framing, focal length, depth of field, gaze and caption relations. A political cartoon has caricature, labelling, symbol and juxtaposition. An infographic has visual hierarchy, data selection and the choices hidden in a scale. A student who writes 'the image is powerful' has said nothing a criterion can reward; one who explains how a low camera angle constructs authority has.

The fix is a rotation rather than a reading list. We work through the types a student has not met, one per session, each with a timed analysis and live marking, and keep a running glossary the student owns at the end. It is unglamorous and it is the most reliable mark movement available in this subject. For a family in Ajman budgeting a term, this is the block we would buy first and the one we would buy before the first mock rather than after it.

sections.heading: Paper 1: a text nobody has seen, and a question that is an instruction
paragraphs: The guided analysis paper gives a student a non-literary text they have never read and a guiding question that tells them what to do with it. Standard Level candidates handle one text in an hour and a quarter; Higher Level candidates handle two in two and a quarter hours and must analyse both. Each analysis is marked out of twenty across the four criteria at five marks each, so one weak analysis at Higher Level cannot be rescued by a strong one.

Three failure modes account for most of the loss. The first is summarising: a candidate retells the text, perhaps elegantly, without ever explaining how it works on a reader. The second is ignoring the guiding question, which is treated as a theme to mention rather than as the spine of the answer. The third is running out of time at Higher Level, because a student spends seventy minutes on the text they liked and thirty on the other.

What a session fixes here is specific. We teach a reading procedure that takes twelve minutes and produces an annotated text with a thesis already visible; we teach how to convert a guiding question into three paragraph claims; and we practise splitting the Higher Level time evenly even when one text is more appealing. Then it is volume. One timed analysis a week with honest marking beats any amount of discussion about what analysis is, and an Ajman student who starts that routine in September has written thirty of them before the first mock.

sections.heading: Paper 2: a comparison written from memory
paragraphs: The comparative essay asks one general question, chosen from four, answered by comparing two literary works studied during the course. The texts are not available in the examination room, which changes the preparation entirely: a student needs quotations in memory, a usable sense of each work's structure, and a stock of comparison points that can be bent to whichever of the four questions fits best.

Candidates lose marks in a pattern so consistent it is almost a signature. The first two paragraphs compare genuinely; the third describes one work; the fourth describes the other; the conclusion asserts that both works explore the theme. Criterion B rewards sustained analysis and evaluation, and an essay that stops comparing has stopped answering. The second common loss is a question answered in general terms about theme, with the works used as illustration rather than as evidence.

A session on Paper 2 is mostly structural. We build a comparison grid for the two works the school has actually taught, decide in advance which pairings serve which likely question types, and then practise writing paragraphs that hold both works in view at once. Memorised quotation banks are homework rather than paid time, and a parent can test them in ten minutes. For Ajman students whose school teaches an unusual pairing of works, this is where an independent reader matters most, because the grid has to be built for those two texts and nobody else's, and no published revision guide will have done it for them.

sections.heading: The Individual Oral: forty marks, two extracts, one global issue
paragraphs: The Individual Oral is fifteen minutes: ten minutes of presentation and five minutes of questions from the teacher. The student chooses a global issue, then one literary extract and one non-literary extract of no more than forty lines each, and explores how each text presents that issue. It is forty marks across the same four criteria at ten marks each, and it is the component most sensitive to a single early decision.

That decision is the global issue. A student who chooses something enormous — inequality, identity, the environment — has set themselves an impossible ten minutes, because nothing specific can be shown in either extract. A student who chooses something narrow and real, such as how a particular kind of migrant worker is represented, or how grief is permitted to be expressed by men, can do close analysis in both extracts and still have time to connect them. We spend the first rehearsal session almost entirely on narrowing, and it is the highest-value hour in the block.

The rest of the rehearsal is mechanical and useful. Both extracts must be analysed, not mentioned; the structure must leave time for the second one; and the five minutes of questions reward a student who has thought about what a teacher might reasonably ask rather than one who has memorised a script. Our tutors do not write the oral and do not choose the extracts; they ask whether the issue can be shown in those lines, and they make the student answer.

sections.heading: The Higher Level essay: 1,500 words that start in the portfolio
paragraphs: Higher Level candidates write a formal essay of 1,200 to 1,500 words on one literary work or one non-literary body of work studied during the course, worth twenty marks across the four criteria at five each. The requirement that shapes everything is that the essay must develop from the learner portfolio. An essay invented from nothing in the final fortnight is possible to submit and very difficult to write well, because the thinking has not happened anywhere.

The line of inquiry is where the grade is set. A line of inquiry is a question narrow enough to be answered in 1,500 words with close reading of one text. Most first attempts are topics: 'the theme of power in the novel', 'the use of imagery'. Those produce essays that survey rather than argue, and criterion B caps them. A good inquiry is uncomfortable and specific, and arriving at one usually takes two sessions of being asked why the current version is not a question.

What a tutor may do here is tightly bounded and we hold the boundary. We question the inquiry, test whether the chosen text can sustain it, point out where an argument claims more than its evidence supports, explain what each criterion is asking for, and read one full draft leaving questions in the margin. We do not supply arguments, rewrite sentences, choose the text, or hand over a structure. Our tutors do not write a student's essay, and we say so because work produced by somebody else puts the student's whole Diploma at risk.

sections.heading: Criterion language: what the mark scheme means by convincing
paragraphs: The four criteria use a small set of words to separate bands, and students who do not know what those words mean cannot aim at them. Criterion A moves from 'adequate' through 'good' to 'perceptive' understanding. Criterion B moves from 'descriptive' through 'adequate' to 'insightful and convincing' analysis and evaluation. Criterion C rewards organisation that is 'mostly' coherent, then 'coherent and effective'. Criterion D asks for language that is 'mostly clear' and then 'very clear, effective, carefully chosen and precise'.

Translated into practice, those words have concrete tests. 'Perceptive' means the interpretation notices something a careful reader might miss and supports it. 'Convincing' in criterion B means every claim about an authorial choice is followed by its effect on a reader, in the same sentence or the next. 'Coherent' in criterion C means a reader can state the argument of each paragraph from its first line. 'Precise' in criterion D means the terms are the right technical ones, used correctly, rather than approximate praise.

Teaching those four tests is the single most portable thing we do in this subject, because the criteria are reused across all four components. A student who learns to follow each feature with its effect has improved Paper 1, Paper 2, the oral and the Higher Level essay at once. That is why a term of honest criterion-based marking is worth more than a term of discussion, and why we mark in the document rather than talking about marking.

sections.heading: The portfolio nobody marks, and why it still decides a grade
paragraphs: The learner portfolio is mandatory and unassessed, which is an awkward combination for a seventeen-year-old. It records a student's engagement with each text studied: notes, responses, trial paragraphs, questions that occurred to them. No mark is attached to it, no examiner reads it, and the Higher Level essay is required to develop from it. Students work out the first three facts quickly and discover the fourth in the second year.

A thin portfolio produces a predictable sequence. The essay deadline arrives, the student has no recorded thinking about any text, so they pick whichever work they remember best and invent a line of inquiry from the title. That inquiry has not been tested against the text, the essay surveys rather than argues, and criterion B does the rest. We can see a thin portfolio in the first ten minutes of a Higher Level essay session, and there is no cheap repair for it in March.

The intervention that works is early and almost free. One portfolio entry per text, written while the text is being taught, containing a question the student actually finds interesting and two pieces of evidence that bear on it. Twenty minutes per text, unpaid, supervised by a parent who asks to see it. For Ajman families who contact us during the first Diploma year, this is the recommendation we lead with, and it saves considerably more than it costs, because nothing we can sell in the second year substitutes for thinking that was never written down.

sections.heading: What an hour fixes, what it costs, and how it reaches Ajman
paragraphs: An honest list. One weekly hour fixes unseen analysis technique, the structure of a comparative paragraph, the narrowing of a global issue, the framing of a line of inquiry, and a student's reading of criterion language. It does not fix a student who has not read the works, it does not generate a portfolio retrospectively, and it does not substitute for memorised quotation. Where a family asks us to make up two years of unread novels in eight weeks, we say plainly that we cannot.

On price, the published UAE market runs from AED 45–65 an hour at EdFlik's entry tier and AED 33–52 at Tutopiya's, through AED 150–300 for a qualified subject teacher online with Unitors listing IB subjects from AED 200, to AED 200–450 and above for an IB specialist, with TutorChase at AED 270 and BartyED at AED 650. Visiting tutors are published at AED 180–500 an hour with travel included. Those are their figures, read in October 2026; IB Gram publishes no hourly list of its own.

Delivery is online, one-to-one, over live video. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE — visiting tuition is a service we run only in India. For this subject the format is a genuine advantage: a timed analysis is written and marked inside the same document, an oral rehearsal can be recorded and played back, and the comparison grid for the school's own two works is built on a shared screen and kept by the student. One further point worth naming: an individual providing private lessons in the UAE needs the MoHRE private tuition work permit introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, issued free of charge for two years, and it is a fair question to ask anybody before you pay them.

process.title: Send a marked script and the works list
process.description: One recent marked analysis or essay, plus the two literary works the school has taught and the date of the Individual Oral recording window. Those three inputs decide the component to aim at and the tutor to propose. A quote produced without the works list is a guess about the most important variable.

process.title: Get a component diagnosis
process.description: We read the script against the criteria and name what is costing marks: summarising instead of analysing, comparison collapsing, criterion B absent, or simply unread texts. Where the honest answer is that the student needs to read rather than to be taught, we say that before quoting anything.

process.title: A free first lesson with the proposed tutor
process.description: A full session before any payment. Ask the tutor to mark one analysis in front of your child, naming the band for each of the four criteria and the reason. That request separates a specialist from a general English tutor in about ten minutes.

process.title: Agree the block, the slot and what is included
process.description: You see the figure, whether marking time is billed separately, and whether the quote includes tax. We fix the Gulf Standard Time slot, the holiday pauses, and post-Iftar timings during Ramadan. Nothing starts until that is written down and agreed.

process.title: Write, mark, keep
process.description: Each session produces a piece of timed writing marked in a document the student keeps, plus a short written note of what was covered. For Higher Level essay hours that note is also the record a school may ask for when confirming the work is the student's own.

process.title: Re-aim after the next school assessment
process.description: When the next internal mark arrives we compare it with the plan rather than with our original diagnosis. Hours move between unseen analysis, the comparative essay and the oral, or stop. A group one plan that looks identical in October and in March was not built on evidence.

whyPoints.title: Marked against the criteria, not praised
whyPoints.description: Every piece of writing comes back with a band and a reason for each of the four criteria. Encouragement is pleasant and does not move a grade. A student who learns that criterion B wants an effect after every named choice improves all four components at once, which is the whole leverage of this subject.

whyPoints.title: An independent second reader
whyPoints.description: In an Ajman department of one or two English teachers, a student has only ever been marked by the person who taught them. A reader who did not choose the works and did not set the task gives a genuinely different calibration, and that is what most families here are buying.

whyPoints.title: The non-literary half gets equal time
whyPoints.description: Paper 1 is drawn entirely from non-literary text types and is the largest block of marks at both levels. We rotate deliberately through photographs, cartoons, infographics and speeches rather than returning to advertisements, and the student keeps the glossary at the end.

whyPoints.title: The academic-honesty line is explicit
whyPoints.description: Tutors question a line of inquiry, test a global issue, mark drafts against criteria and ask awkward questions. They do not write essays, supply arguments, choose extracts or rewrite sentences. Completed coursework is sold openly in this market, and a student who submits it risks their whole Diploma.

whyPoints.title: Scheduling built for a northern-emirates week
whyPoints.description: Late weekday slots for households commuting from Sharjah or Dubai, Saturday blocks long enough for timed writing and its marking, and post-Iftar timings during Ramadan at no surcharge. Sessions pause for school holidays without losing the slot.

whyPoints.title: Clear about what we are not
whyPoints.description: IB Gram is an independent matching platform with no approval, licence or endorsement from any authority or examination board, no premises in the UAE, and no tutor sent to a UAE address. We promise no grade, and every AED figure here names the company that published it.

faqs.question: My son reads constantly and still gets a 4 in English A. What is going on?
faqs.answer: Almost always criterion B. Language and Literature rewards explaining what an authorial choice does to a reader, in the same breath as naming it. A strong reader who retells a text accurately, however elegantly, sits in the middle bands because interpretation and evaluation are being assessed rather than comprehension. The second common cause is the unseen paper: half the course is non-literary text types, and most students have practised two of them. Send one marked analysis and the pattern is usually obvious within ten minutes of reading it.

faqs.question: How many works does my child study at Standard and Higher Level in this course?
faqs.answer: Standard Level studies four literary works and two non-literary bodies of work. Higher Level studies six literary works and three non-literary bodies of work. The school chooses which, within the IB's requirements for the three areas of exploration, so two students in different Ajman schools can be sitting the same examination having read entirely different novels. Ask the Diploma coordinator for the works list before booking any tuition, because the comparative essay preparation has to be built for those specific texts and is not transferable.

faqs.question: Why does my daughter analyse novels well but lose marks on the unseen Paper 1 text?
faqs.answer: Because the two tasks are not the same skill. A novel is analysed over weeks with a teacher's framing available; an unseen non-literary text has to be read, annotated and argued about in a single sitting, against a guiding question. Students who have mainly practised advertisements and opinion columns then meet a photograph or an infographic and have no vocabulary for it. The repair is a rotation through unpractised text types, one timed analysis a week, marked against the criteria. It is the most reliable mark movement available in this subject.

faqs.question: Which non-literary bodies of work will my child in Ajman be studying?
faqs.answer: The school chooses them, so ask the Diploma coordinator. The term means a connected set of non-literary texts by one author, organisation or source: a photographer's portfolio, a columnist's pieces, a campaign's advertisements, a cartoonist's work, a brand's communications. Standard Level studies two such bodies and Higher Level three, and they supply material for the Individual Oral and, at Higher Level, a possible essay subject. Paper 1 draws on unseen texts rather than these, but the analytical vocabulary built while studying a body of work is exactly what the unseen paper rewards, which is why it is worth studying properly.

faqs.question: Can my child take the novels into the Paper 2 examination?
faqs.answer: No. The comparative essay is written without the literary works available, which changes the preparation completely. A student needs quotations held in memory, a usable sense of each work's structure and a stock of comparison points flexible enough to serve whichever of the four general questions fits best. Memorising quotation is homework rather than paid tutoring time. What a session is worth doing is building the comparison grid for the two works the school has actually taught, then practising paragraphs that hold both texts in view at once.

faqs.question: How long may each Individual Oral extract run, and who chooses them?
faqs.answer: Each extract may be no more than forty lines, and the student chooses both: one from a literary work studied and one from a non-literary body of work studied. The pair has to demonstrate the global issue the student has selected, which is why the choosing and the narrowing happen together. A tutor may ask whether a particular issue can actually be shown in those forty lines and make the student answer, but the extracts and the issue remain the student's own decisions, and so does every word of the presentation.

faqs.question: What makes a global issue narrow enough for a ten-minute oral?
faqs.answer: A good test: can you show it happening inside forty lines of text, twice? Inequality, identity and the environment fail that test, because nothing specific appears in either extract and the student ends up talking about the world rather than the texts. How a particular group of workers is represented, or how grief is permitted to be expressed by men, passes it. Narrowing is the highest-value hour in an oral rehearsal block, and it is the first thing we spend time on, because every criterion downstream depends on it.

faqs.question: Is the learner portfolio actually marked by anyone?
faqs.answer: No, and that is precisely why it causes trouble. The portfolio is mandatory and unassessed, and the Higher Level essay is required to develop from it. Students reasonably conclude it does not matter and then reach the essay deadline with no recorded thinking about any text, so they invent a line of inquiry from a title. One entry per text written while that text is taught, containing a real question and two pieces of evidence, takes twenty minutes and prevents the whole sequence. It is free, and a parent can supervise it.

faqs.question: How long is the Higher Level essay and what can it be written about?
faqs.answer: Between 1,200 and 1,500 words, on one literary work or one non-literary body of work studied during the course, developed from the learner portfolio and answering a line of inquiry the student frames. It carries twenty marks across the four criteria at five each. The grade is largely set by the inquiry: a question narrow enough to answer with close reading of one text scores; a topic such as the use of imagery produces a survey, and criterion B caps it. Expect two sessions on the inquiry alone.

faqs.question: What does the mark scheme mean when it asks for convincing analysis?
faqs.answer: In criterion B, convincing means that every authorial choice named is followed by its effect on a reader, close enough that the connection is unmistakable. Identifying a device and moving on is descriptive and sits in the lower bands. The equivalent tests for the other criteria are just as concrete: perceptive interpretation notices something a careful reader might miss and proves it, coherent organisation lets a reader state each paragraph's argument from its first line, and precise language uses the correct technical term rather than approximate praise.

faqs.question: Our Ajman school has one English A teacher. Does that affect my child's grade?
faqs.answer: Not directly, and indirectly it matters. A single-teacher department means one marking voice, one set of chosen works and no second calibration, so a student who receives 13 out of 20 has no way of knowing whether that is generous or harsh against the published bands. The practical consequence is a surprise in the final results rather than a gradual correction. An independent reader who did not teach the class and did not set the task is the service most families in this emirate are actually buying from us.

faqs.question: Does an English tutor need a government permit to charge us in the UAE?
faqs.answer: Yes. An individual providing private lessons needs the private tuition work permit introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, issued through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation free of charge for two years. The MoHRE service is listed as Issuance of a New Work Permit — Private Tutor Licensing, with a two-working-day completion time and no published fee. Registered teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and students aged 15 to 18 may apply. Tutoring without one attracts fines and penalties under the applicable laws.

faqs.question: What does group one English tuition cost in the UAE market?
faqs.answer: Published figures read in October 2026 run from AED 45–65 an hour at EdFlik's entry tier and AED 33–52 at Tutopiya's, through AED 150–300 for a qualified subject teacher online with Unitors listing IB subjects from AED 200, to AED 200–450 and above for a specialist, with TutorChase at AED 270 and BartyED at AED 650. Visiting tutors are published at AED 180–500 including travel. Those belong to the companies that published them. IB Gram publishes no hourly list; the free first lesson precedes any figure being agreed.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send an English tutor to an address in Ajman?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; visiting tuition is a service we run only in India. Lessons for Ajman families run one-to-one over live video, which suits this subject unusually well: a timed analysis is written and marked inside the same document, an oral rehearsal can be recorded and replayed against the criteria, and the comparison grid for the school's own two works stays with the student. The local visiting market does exist at a published AED 180–500 an hour if proximity is essential for your child.

faqs.question: What may a tutor do with the Higher Level essay without breaking IB rules?
faqs.answer: Question the line of inquiry until it becomes a real question, test whether the chosen text can sustain it, explain what each criterion asks for, point out where an argument claims more than its evidence supports, and read one full draft leaving questions in the margin. What a tutor may not do is supply arguments, rewrite sentences, choose the text or hand over a structure. Our tutors do not write a student's essay. Work produced by somebody else is a malpractice finding against the student, and it puts the whole Diploma at risk.

intro.heading: The one Diploma component with a built-in audit trail
paragraphs: Most of what a parent in Ajman buys in education is invisible until a grade arrives. The Extended Essay is the exception, because the IB has already built the evidence into the assessment. A student must hold three reflection sessions with a school supervisor, record roughly 500 words of reflection across them on a form the supervisor countersigns, and complete a concluding interview known as the viva voce. Those documented reflections are assessed in their own right and carry six of the 34 available marks.

That changes what this page needs to be. There is no need to invent a progress report when the IB mandates one. The useful work is reading the trail that exists: the research question as first registered and as it now stands, the reflections in the student's own words, the supervisor's comment, the current word count against the ceiling, and a draft audited for the one criterion that carries twelve marks. All of that is readable in a single session, and most of it is readable by a parent.

Ajman adds specifics worth planning around. Private schools here are supervised by the federal Ministry of Education rather than an emirate regulator, so internal deadlines are set school by school, and many Ajman students attend campuses in Sharjah or Dubai and follow that calendar instead. The emirate's Diploma cohort is small, which means a supervisor may be carrying essays across several subject groups at once. Mentoring that reads the trail and feeds the supervisor rather than competing with them is the arrangement that works.

Delivery is one-to-one over live video. IB Gram does not send a mentor to an address in Ajman or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service offered only in India. For a research project that is less of a compromise than it sounds, because almost all of the work is a student reading sources and a mentor reading what the student wrote. Screen sharing a draft and a criterion descriptor side by side is in several ways better than two people leaning over one printed page.

The sections that follow take the trail apart in order. Where the 34 marks sit and which of them a late intervention can still reach. The research question log, and what each abandoned version costs in weeks. What the 4,000-word count includes and excludes, which routinely surprises families. How the three reflections and the viva voce are actually assessed. What Ajman students can realistically access for primary data. And the single point in the process where a mentor must refuse, whatever the deadline looks like. Ajman families also want to know how a mentor works alongside a school supervisor without stepping on the role the IB reserves for them, and that boundary is set out below before anything else.

ajman/ib-dp-extended-essay-tutor.programmesIntro: The Extended Essay sits in the Diploma core, but the research habits it assesses are introduced earlier in the IB continuum. Below is what each programme contributes and what that means for an Ajman student's starting point.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: A 4,000-word independent research essay registered in one approved subject, supervised in school, and marked by an external examiner against five criteria worth 34 marks in total. Alongside it sit three mandatory reflection sessions, a reflection form of roughly 500 words, and a concluding viva voce. The grade combines with Theory of Knowledge in a matrix worth up to three bonus points on the Diploma total.
programmes.countryNote: Ajman Diploma students are often supervised by a teacher whose own subject sits elsewhere, simply because the cohort is small. That is permitted and common, and it shifts the burden of subject-specific source evaluation onto the student. It is also the single clearest case for an external reader who knows the registered subject, since the supervisor's recommended three to five hours cannot cover everything.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: The MYP Personal Project is the first graded independent project most IB students produce, and the first time a process journal is assessed rather than just the outcome. Criterion-referenced marking, a documented plan and a reflection on the result are all rehearsals for the Extended Essay's reflection requirement, which catches students out when they meet it for the first time in DP1.
programmes.countryNote: An Ajman student arriving in DP1 from Ajman Academy's MYP will already have produced a process journal and will recognise why the reflections carry marks. A student arriving from an Indian or British Year 11 route usually will not, and tends to treat the reflection form as paperwork until someone shows them it is worth six marks.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: The Career-related Programme replaces the Extended Essay with a reflective project tied to an ethical dilemma from the student's career-related study. It is shorter, differently assessed, and does not feed the bonus point matrix. Mentioned here because families comparing IB routes in the northern emirates occasionally assume the research requirement is identical across all three IB options at this age.
programmes.countryNote: Very few schools in Ajman or the neighbouring emirates run the Career-related Programme, so an Ajman family weighing IB routes is almost always choosing between the full Diploma and a British or Indian curriculum. If a student does move onto CP mid-course, the research work already done is not wasted but the assessment criteria change completely.

ajman/ib-dp-extended-essay-tutor.subjectsIntro: An Extended Essay is registered in one subject, and that choice sets the ceiling on criteria A and C before any reading happens. Below are the registrations Ajman students most often choose, with the practical constraint each one carries in this emirate.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Strong essays need either controlled primary data or a genuinely narrow literature question. Laboratory access in a small school is the limiting factor, and field data from Al Zorah's mangroves is a realistic Ajman alternative, provided the sampling method is defensible and the permissions are in order.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: The commonest failure is a question that needs equipment the school does not hold. A workable Ajman variant uses water hardness or chloride content in locally available supplies, where the apparatus is simple and the uncertainty discussion is where criterion C marks are won.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Rewards narrow questions with clean measurement. Essays that start from a broad phenomenon almost always score low on focus and method. An Ajman student with access to nothing more than a phone sensor and a careful method can outscore one with a borrowed laboratory and a vague question.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: The emirate offers unusually accessible material: free zone activity, cross-border labour flows into Sharjah and Dubai, and port and logistics data. The risk is a question that becomes a description of a market. Criterion C demands that theory is applied and then tested against the evidence, not illustrated by it.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Primary interviews are easy to arrange in Ajman's small-business sector and hard to use well. One interview with a named manager, analysed against a framework, beats five interviews summarised. Consent and data handling need stating in the methodology, not assumed.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: The subject where source evaluation carries the essay. Questions must be at least ten years old to qualify, which rules out most contemporary UAE topics. Trucial States material, federation-era documents and the pre-oil pearling economy are viable and archivally served.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Needs a question about how a text works rather than what it means. Students who choose two texts without a comparative justification lose focus marks immediately. The advantage is that no equipment, data or permission is required, which suits a late start better than a science.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.description: The highest-ceiling and highest-risk registration. A mathematics essay must contain genuine mathematics developed by the student, not an exposition of a known result. Where it works, criterion C scores well because the reasoning is explicit and auditable on the page.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Ethical constraints prevent most primary research at this level, so the essay lives or dies on how studies are compared. The strongest ones interrogate method and sample rather than listing findings, which is exactly the critical thinking the twelve-mark criterion is looking for.

subjects.name: World Studies
subjects.description: Two subjects applied to one issue of global significance, with a local case. An Ajman student can anchor a World Studies essay in migration, water security or coastal development, but the interdisciplinary justification must be argued explicitly or the essay reads as two half essays stapled together.

subjects.name: Arabic A or Arabic B
subjects.description: Available and underused by Ajman students who speak Arabic at home. Supervision in the registered language is the practical constraint, since a small school may have nobody free to read it. Worth asking the coordinator early rather than discovering the gap in DP2.

subjects.name: Visual Arts
subjects.description: A written research essay, not a portfolio. Students frequently register expecting to submit artwork and then find they must argue about interpretation and context. Local material is available through Ajman's museum collections and the dhow building yards along the creek.

ajman/ib-dp-extended-essay-tutor.regionsIntro: Where a family lives in Ajman changes two things for a research project: when a session can start, and what primary data is physically reachable. Both are worth deciding before the research question is registered.

regions.name: Ajman Corniche and Al Rumailah
regions.note: Waterfront apartments with the shortest school runs in the emirate and the easiest evening slots. Walkable access to the museum quarter and the fish market makes small primary studies in Business Management or Economics genuinely feasible rather than theoretical.

regions.name: Al Nuaimiya
regions.note: The dense older district beside the main school cluster. Students here are mostly on Indian curricula before the Diploma, so the reflection requirement is new to them. Sessions can start early, from about 5pm, because nobody is sitting in Emirates Road traffic.

regions.name: Al Jurf
regions.note: A mixed industrial and residential area with real access to small manufacturers and workshops. That is an advantage for an interview-based registration, provided consent and data handling are written into the methodology rather than arranged informally.

regions.name: Al Mowaihat
regions.note: Villa communities feeding schools in both Ajman and Sharjah. Parents commonly commute to Dubai, which pushes weekday sessions past 7.30pm and makes the weekend block the realistic slot for a long reading session on a draft.

regions.name: Al Zahya and Al Tallah
regions.note: The Emirates Road corridor, where most students attend campuses across the Sharjah boundary. Their internal submission dates follow that school, so the backwards calendar on this page should be rebuilt from the supervisor's sheet rather than assumed.

regions.name: Al Zorah
regions.note: Mangrove and lagoon habitat on the northern edge of the city, and the emirate's one readily accessible field site. Useful for a Biology or Environmental Systems registration, with the caveat that any sampling needs permission and a method that survives examiner scrutiny.

regions.name: Al Helio and Al Rawda
regions.note: Established residential districts where many students are the first in the family through an IB Diploma. The reflection form is usually where support is most needed, because nobody at home has seen one before and schools rarely explain its mark weighting.

regions.name: Masfout and Manama
regions.note: The inland exclaves, over an hour from the coast and agriculturally distinct from the rest of the emirate. Interesting territory for a geography or economics question about water and farming, and the clearest case for remote mentoring, since no specialist market exists at that distance.

schoolClusters.city: The Ajman city cluster
schoolClusters.note: Schools around Al Nuaimiya, Al Rashidiya and Al Jurf, mostly Indian and British curricula. Diploma students here typically arrive from Year 11 or Class 10 and meet an assessed reflection process for the first time with the Extended Essay.
schools: GEMS Our Own English High School, Ajman
Ibn Seena English High School, Ajman

schoolClusters.city: The Emirates Road campuses
schoolClusters.note: Newer schools serving Al Zahya, Al Tallah and Al Mowaihat, including the emirate's IB continuum provision. Students from this cluster usually arrive with MYP process journals behind them and need less help understanding why reflections are marked.

schoolClusters.city: Campuses across the Sharjah and Dubai border
schoolClusters.note: A large share of Ajman Diploma students cross an emirate boundary every morning, which means their supervisor, their internal deadlines and their library access all belong to another school system. Any plan should be built from that school's sheet.
schools: The International School of Creative Science, Sharjah
