ajman/ib-dp-theory-of-knowledge-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below read Diploma core work for a living: TOK commentaries, prescribed title plans and essay drafts. Each one marks against the published instrument, writes the band on the page, and explains which sentence cost the mark. Ask for a sample of returned work before you book anything.

intro.heading: Ask for the marked draft before you ask for the price
paragraphs: Theory of Knowledge is the one Diploma subject where a parent in Ajman cannot tell from the outside whether anything is improving. There is no textbook chapter to test, no past paper to score out of 80, no weekly vocabulary list. A student says the lesson was interesting, the term ends, and a predicted grade arrives that nobody saw coming. That is why this page is built around evidence rather than method. The useful question to ask any TOK tutor is not what they teach but what they hand back.

What a TOK session should leave behind is an artefact. A written exhibition commentary with marks against each of the three objects. A prescribed title plan with the command words circled and the two areas of knowledge named. An essay draft with band comments in the margin and a global band at the top, matched to the wording of the TOK assessment instrument the IB publishes for examiners. None of that is exotic. It is simply the difference between a conversation and a record.

Ajman adds a practical layer. Private schools here sit under the federal Ministry of Education rather than a Dubai or Abu Dhabi regulator, the IB Diploma cohort in the emirate is small, and a large share of families commute to work in Dubai or Sharjah. The result is late evenings and a thin local pool of teachers who have marked TOK against the real instrument. A specialist reached over video solves the second problem; scheduling on Gulf Standard Time after 7pm solves the first. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE, so there is no travel window to lose.

The other reason to insist on marked work is that TOK carries a failing condition. A grade E in Theory of Knowledge, or in the Extended Essay, prevents the award of the Diploma whatever the subject points say. Pairs of letters from the two core components also feed a bonus point matrix worth up to three points on the final total. A family that can see band movement across a term can judge whether a C is drifting towards a D or climbing towards a B. A family relying on impressions cannot, and by the time a predicted grade lands the room for repair has usually gone.

So the sections below do two jobs. They explain, in the IB's own terms, how the exhibition and the essay are scored, what the bands actually describe and where Ajman students lose marks most often. Then they show the week-by-week record a Diploma core support plan in Ajman should generate: who produced what, who scored it, and what changed. If a tutor cannot produce that record, the lessons may still be pleasant. They are not measurable.

ajman/ib-dp-theory-of-knowledge-tutor.programmesIntro: Theory of Knowledge belongs to the Diploma Programme, but the habits it assesses are built earlier. Below is how each IB programme an Ajman family might be inside contributes to the core, and what that means for when support is worth starting.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: The two-year Diploma carries three core elements alongside six subjects: Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. TOK is assessed by an internally marked exhibition of three objects with a commentary capped at 950 words, and an externally marked essay of up to 1,600 words on one of six prescribed titles released by the IB for each session. The essay counts for two-thirds of the TOK grade.
programmes.countryNote: The Ajman IB Diploma Programme cohort is small enough that a school may run TOK with one teacher across both year groups, often in a timetable slot that gets borrowed for other things. Families here frequently find the exhibition has been completed in a rush. Ajman Academy is the emirate's IB continuum school; several Ajman families also register at IB schools in Sharjah and Dubai and commute, which changes the internal deadline calendar.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: MYP assessment is criterion-referenced, and two of its habits transfer directly into TOK: justifying a claim with evidence, and evaluating the method that produced the evidence. A student who has written MYP criterion D responses has already argued about the limits of knowledge without using the phrase. The Personal Project is the first long independent piece most IB students produce and the first place process documentation is graded.
programmes.countryNote: An MYP student in Ajman moving into DP1 the following August is the ideal moment to start core support, because the exhibition lands early in DP1 while subject content is still light. Work from the Personal Project is useful raw material for a first diagnostic: it shows whether the student can hold a line of argument across pages rather than paragraphs.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: PYP ends with the Exhibition, a collaborative inquiry presented to the school community. The naming is a coincidence, but the demand is related: a student selects a line of inquiry, gathers sources, and explains to an audience why the question matters. PYP also introduces the transdisciplinary skills that TOK later makes explicit, including how a claim is supported and who is entitled to make it.
programmes.countryNote: Only a small number of Ajman schools run PYP, so most Diploma students in the emirate arrive from British or Indian primary routes rather than from the IB continuum. That matters for TOK because those students meet criterion-referenced marking for the first time in DP1, and the vocabulary of the TOK instrument is genuinely new to them rather than a familiar register.

ajman/ib-dp-theory-of-knowledge-tutor.subjectsIntro: A TOK essay is only as good as the examples carrying it, and the strongest examples come from subjects the student already studies. Below are the subjects Ajman Diploma students most often draw on, and what each one contributes to a TOK argument when it is used properly rather than named.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: Two assessed tasks, graded A to E. Marks are awarded against a single global instrument for each task, not a checklist, which is why a draft can be factually correct and still sit in the 5-6 band. The instrument rewards sustained, evaluated argument about how knowledge is produced in named areas of knowledge.

subjects.name: The Extended Essay
subjects.description: The other half of the bonus point matrix, and the component most often supported by the same mentor. A student who has handled source evaluation for a History or Biology research question already has the material for a TOK paragraph on method and reliability, and the two components reinforce each other when planned together.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: The richest source of TOK examples, because historiography is explicit about perspective and evidence. A student who can explain why two accounts of the same event differ, and what each historian had access to, has the backbone of an argument about knowledge in the human sciences and history as areas of knowledge.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Supplies method examples that work: replication, sample size, control variables, and the gap between correlation and cause. An Ajman student whose Biology IA involved an unreliable data set can use it as a first-hand knowledge claim, which is far stronger in TOK than a textbook anecdote about a famous experiment.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Useful for the problem of models. Students meet several incompatible atomic models in sequence and are asked to use each where it works. That is a concrete route into questions about whether a model is true or merely useful, which the natural sciences area of knowledge rewards when argued with a specific case.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: The home of measurement uncertainty. A student who has propagated error through a calculation can discuss the limits of precision without hand-waving, and can contrast that with the certainty claimed in mathematics. Strong TOK essays often sit on exactly this comparison between two areas of knowledge.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Proof is the one place in the Diploma where certainty is available, which makes mathematics the natural contrast class in a TOK essay. Students who have worked through a proof by induction can say what a proof guarantees and what it does not, rather than repeating that maths is objective.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Models with assumptions baked in, applied to messy evidence. Ajman students often have good local material here, from free zone activity to fuel pricing, and a TOK paragraph grounded in a case they can describe outperforms a generic reference to behavioural economics.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Trains the close reading that the prescribed titles demand. Students who have analysed how a text positions a reader are better at noticing that a title says knowledge rather than facts, or replication rather than repetition, and that the wording restricts what counts as an answer.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: The clearest case of knowledge produced under ethical constraint. Students can discuss why certain studies cannot be repeated and what that does to the evidence base, which is a sharper human sciences argument than the usual description of a famous obedience experiment.

subjects.name: Arabic B and Arabic ab initio
subjects.description: Relevant beyond language acquisition for Ajman students, because Arabic, Islamic Education and social studies run alongside the licensed curriculum in UAE private schools under federal rules. Students who study knowledge in two languages have genuine material on translation and the limits of shared concepts.

subjects.name: Visual Arts
subjects.description: The arts area of knowledge is the one most often handled badly, usually because students assert that art expresses feeling and stop. A student with a comparative study behind them can instead discuss how an interpretation is justified, and who in a community of artists and critics decides that it holds.

sections.heading: What a marked TOK draft actually looks like when it comes back
paragraphs: A marked TOK draft returned by a competent reader has four things on it, and a parent in Ajman can check all four without knowing the subject. First, a global band, written as a range out of ten with the instrument's own wording quoted beside it. Second, margin comments that name the fault rather than the feeling, so not awkward but claim asserted, no counterclaim or example named but not used. Third, a short list at the end of changes in priority order. Fourth, a date.

That last item is the one families overlook and the one that makes the record work. Three dated drafts across a term tell you whether the student is moving. A single undated draft tells you nothing, and a set of verbal impressions tells you less. The TOK assessment instrument the IB publishes for its examiners is a global impression tool with five bands, each described in a paragraph rather than a tick list, which is precisely why the band needs to be written down and justified in words a student can act on.

The commonest disappointment is a draft returned with corrected grammar and a comment saying it reads well. Prose quality is not what either TOK task rewards. The instrument asks whether the discussion is sustained, whether the arguments are evaluated, whether claims are supported by specific examples, and whether the response stays with the title or the prompt as written. A draft can be elegant and sit in the 3-4 band because every paragraph describes a position without weighing it.

So the first thing to ask an IB DP Theory of Knowledge tutor in Ajman for is not a plan but a sample of returned work with the student's name removed. If the sample carries a band, reasoning tied to the instrument, and an ordered list of fixes, the tutor marks. If it carries ticks and encouragement, they do not.

sections.heading: The exhibition commentary, read as evidence rather than as a task
paragraphs: The TOK exhibition asks a student to choose one of 35 internal assessment prompts, select three specific objects, and explain in a commentary of no more than 950 words how each object connects to that prompt. It is marked in school against the instrument and moderated by the IB, and it contributes one third of the TOK grade. Most Ajman students complete it during DP1, often faster than they should.

Reading an existing TOK exhibition commentary as evidence takes about fifteen minutes and is the cheapest diagnostic available. Three checks do most of the work. Is each object specific, with a real provenance, rather than a category? A particular prayer rug in a particular family, with a date and a story, is an object; prayer rugs in general is a topic. Does each commentary paragraph answer the chosen prompt in its exact wording, or does it drift to a neighbouring question? And is the word budget distributed, roughly 300 words to each object, rather than 600 on the favourite and 150 on the last?

The failures cluster. Students pick objects they can describe instead of objects that argue, which produces three paragraphs of description and a band in the middle. Students change the prompt's wording slightly and answer the question they prefer. Students use a photograph of something generic found online, which strips away the provenance the commentary needs. Each of these is visible on the page, which means it is fixable in one session and verifiable in the next version.

Local objects work well here and are underused. An Ajman student has access to material nobody in a marking pile has seen: a dhow builder's tool from the creek, a federal textbook page in Arabic alongside its English counterpart, a utility bill showing a desalinated water charge. The object does not need to be impressive. It needs to be specific, locatable, and genuinely connected to the prompt the student chose.

sections.heading: The prescribed title plan: the artefact worth producing first
paragraphs: Six prescribed titles are released by the IB for each examination session, and the student answers one of them without altering a word. The essay runs to a maximum of 1,600 words, is marked by an external examiner, and carries two thirds of the TOK grade. Almost every recoverable mark on that essay is decided before any prose exists, in the plan, which is why the plan is the first artefact a session should produce.

A usable plan fits on one page and has five parts. The title copied exactly, with the command terms and the restricting words underlined. A gloss of each key term in the student's own words, because a title that says knowledge rather than information is restricting what counts as an answer. Two named areas of knowledge that genuinely pull in different directions. For each, one real example the student can describe in detail from their own subjects or life. And a counterclaim per area, with its own evidence rather than a sentence of concession.

A plan like that is markable. A tutor can look at it and say, honestly, that the second area of knowledge duplicates the first, or that the example named is one the student cannot actually describe, or that the counterclaim is a restatement. Those judgements take ten minutes and save a fortnight. Compare that with the usual sequence, where a student produces 1,600 words from a one-line idea and then gets told the structure is wrong, with the deadline two weeks away.

Some students find the plan harder than the prose, and that is the point. The plan is where the thinking is assessed. A good prescribed title plan also exposes whether the essay should be attempted at all with that title: if the student cannot name two areas of knowledge they can argue about, choosing a different title from the six is a legitimate and much cheaper decision in week one than in week nine.

sections.heading: Twelve weeks of evidence: the record a core support plan should leave
paragraphs: Week by week is not a marketing frame here. It is how a TOK grade is actually built, because both tasks are long-form and assessed on sustained argument rather than recall. A plan that produces one scored artefact a week is also the only way a parent in Ajman can audit progress without reading TOK themselves. The table below is the shape of a real twelve-week run in DP1, aligned to a school's internal exhibition and essay deadlines rather than to any examination date.

Two features of that record matter more than the rest. The scorer column changes: some artefacts are marked by the tutor, some by the school's TOK teacher, and some by the student against the instrument with the tutor checking the self-assessment. A student who can band their own draft within one band of the tutor has learned the instrument, which is the point of the exercise. The evidence column is written as a comparison, not as a compliment, so week nine says counterclaim now carries its own example, previously a single sentence.

The run also plans for the weeks when nothing is produced. Mock fortnight, school trips and the Ramadan timetable change what a student can do, and a record that pretends otherwise is fiction. Sessions in those weeks switch to reading and oral defence of an existing draft, which still generates evidence without demanding new writing. During Ramadan, families in Ajman commonly move the slot after Iftar, which works for a remote tutor and would be awkward for anyone travelling.

At the end of a run like this, the useful output is one document: the band history, the dated artefacts and the open issues. If the student then moves school, changes mentor or needs a predicted grade conversation, that document is the argument. Nothing in it depends on anyone's opinion of how the lessons felt.

sections.heading: Grade movement: what one letter is worth on the Diploma total
paragraphs: TOK and the Extended Essay are graded A to E and combine in a published matrix to award up to three bonus points on the Diploma total of 45. The matrix is not linear, which is why tracking band movement matters more in some positions than others. Moving TOK from C to B is worth a point if the Extended Essay is already at B or above, and worth nothing at all if the essay sits at D. A family watching the record can see which of the two components is the constraint.

The failing condition is the harder number. A grade E in either TOK or the Extended Essay prevents the award of the Diploma regardless of how strong the six subject grades are. That is not a scare tactic; it is a rule a small number of students meet every session, usually because one core component was left too late while subject revision took every available hour. An evidence record is the early warning, because a draft sitting in the 1-2 band in week eight is a visible fact rather than a worry.

The practical consequence for an Ajman family is about where to spend hours. If the record shows TOK at a secure 5-6 band and the Extended Essay unstarted, the hours belong to the essay. If both sit mid-band, the cheaper letter to move is usually TOK, because its two tasks are shorter and the instrument is the same for both. These are decisions you can only make with two scored records side by side, which is the argument for treating Diploma core support in Ajman as one brief rather than two.

Nobody should promise a letter. The honest claim is narrower and more useful: band positions are visible, the faults that cap a band are nameable, and a student who fixes a named fault usually moves. What happens at moderation and external marking is outside anyone's control, and a tutor who talks about certainties rather than bands is telling you something about themselves.

sections.heading: Academic honesty in TOK, and what the evidence file has to show
paragraphs: TOK is where the boundary between support and malpractice is tested hardest, because the output is argument rather than calculation and the help is invisible once the prose is smooth. The IB's position is clear enough to work with: the work submitted must be the student's own, a supervisor or teacher may discuss and give feedback, and only one draft of the essay may be commented on formally before the final version. A tutor operates inside that same rule, not outside it.

What a tutor may legitimately do is read, question, score and explain. Mark a draft against the instrument. Ask why a counterclaim is a single sentence. Point out that an example is named but never used. Explain what the instrument means by evaluated. Teach the student how to self-band. What nobody may do is supply prose, restructure paragraphs on the student's behalf, choose the three objects, or hand over a model answer for adaptation. IB Gram does not produce assessed work for students, and no amount of deadline pressure changes that.

The evidence record helps here rather than hindering. A file of dated drafts in the student's own voice, with margin comments and a visible band history, is exactly what a school wants to see if a question is ever raised. The pattern that looks bad is the opposite: one weak early draft, then a polished final version with no intermediate stages and a register that does not match the student's other work. Keeping version history is as much a protection as a progress tool.

Generative tools sit in the same frame. A student may use them, as they may use any source, and must then acknowledge them properly; what cannot happen is text generated elsewhere appearing as the student's own argument. For TOK specifically there is a practical reason beyond the rule. Machine prose about knowledge questions is fluent, generic and reliably mid-band, because it describes positions instead of weighing them against named examples the student can actually defend in an oral.

sections.heading: Ajman specifics: the Ministry, the commute and the Arabic requirement
paragraphs: Private schools in Ajman are supervised by the federal Ministry of Education, not by an emirate-level authority. The u.ae guidance sets out the regulator map plainly: KHDA covers Dubai, ADEK covers Abu Dhabi and Al Ain, the Sharjah Private Education Authority covers Sharjah, the Department of Knowledge covers Ras Al Khaimah, and the Ministry of Education supervises private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah. For a TOK parent this is mostly administrative, but it changes where an inspection report or a complaint actually goes.

The federal baseline also shapes a Diploma student's week here. Private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, and must observe the Ministry's general regulations. In practice a DP1 student in Ajman is carrying six Diploma subjects, TOK, the Extended Essay, CAS and the mandatory UAE subjects at the same time. Any honest week-by-week plan has to assume fewer free evenings than a plan written for a student in a lighter system.

The commute is the other local fact worth planning around. A large share of Ajman households work in Dubai or Sharjah, and a parent who leaves Al Mowaihat at seven in the morning is rarely home before seven in the evening. That pushes Diploma core sessions to 7.30pm or later on weekdays, with the bigger blocks at weekends. A remote specialist absorbs that easily. A travelling tutor would spend the commute window in traffic and charge for it, which is one reason the in-home market in the northern emirates is thin at Diploma level.

Tutoring itself is permitted but regulated. An individual giving private lessons in the UAE needs a MoHRE private tuition work permit, introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and granted free of charge for two years, with eligibility extending to registered school teachers, government and private sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Those without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No fine schedule has been published, so any figure quoted to you should be treated with scepticism.

sections.heading: What the market charges for Diploma core support, and what to ask before paying
paragraphs: Published rates in the UAE tutoring market spread widely, and Diploma core work sits towards the upper end because the pool of people who have marked TOK against the instrument is small. Budget online providers advertise from around AED 45 to 65 an hour and platform rates from roughly AED 33 to 52, while qualified subject tutors online are commonly quoted between AED 150 and 300. Specialist IB work is quoted at AED 200 to 450 and above, with one named provider publishing AED 650 for premium sessions and an aggregator reporting in-home visits at AED 180 to 350. Those are the market's numbers, attributed to the sources that published them, not a price list.

Two structures dominate. An hourly rate suits the single diagnostic and the weekly record. A project block, quoted from plan to submission, suits the deadline run and is how most Extended Essay support is sold. The trap in the block is scope: a block that includes unlimited reading of successive drafts conflicts with the one-permitted-draft rule, and a block that includes proofreading is selling something a tutor should not deliver. Ask what the block excludes before asking what it costs.

Three questions separate a marker from a conversationalist. Can you show a redacted sample of returned work with a band on it? Do you hold a MoHRE private tuition work permit, and will you say so in writing? What do you refuse to do with a draft? The third answer is the most revealing. A tutor who cannot name a limit has no limit, and a provider advertising finished Internal Assessments or completed essays is selling the student an expulsion risk rather than a grade.

For context, school fees in the region have their own trajectory: KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that private school fees in Dubai would not rise for the 2026-27 academic year under the emirate's economic incentives package. Tutoring is an additional discretionary spend on top of fees, and the evidence record is what tells you whether that spend is doing anything. A family in Ajman buying one scored diagnostic and then deciding is behaving rationally, which is why that option is listed first on this page.

process.title: Send the work that already exists
process.description: Share whatever the student has: a commentary, a title plan, a half-finished draft, or the school's internal deadline sheet. Nothing needs tidying first. A rough draft tells a tutor more than a clean one, because the faults are still visible and the band is honest.

process.title: Take the first lesson at no charge
process.description: A 45-minute session on Gulf Standard Time, scheduled after the Ajman school run and the Dubai or Sharjah commute. The tutor reads the work live, asks the student to defend two claims, and bands what exists. No card details are taken and there is nothing to cancel afterwards.

process.title: Read the marked artefact
process.description: Within a day you receive the scored document: a band out of ten, the instrument's wording quoted against it, margin comments naming each fault, and an ordered list of changes. Decide from that document rather than from a sales conversation whether the match is right.

process.title: Set the record running
process.description: If you continue, each week produces one dated artefact and one score, logged in a single running document. The scorer rotates between tutor, student self-assessment and the school's own marks, so the band history is triangulated rather than one person's view.

process.title: Review at the school's internal deadline
process.description: At the submission point, the band history is closed out with open issues listed. Many families stop there, some continue into the Extended Essay with the same mentor, and either choice is reasonable. Nothing renews automatically and the record belongs to you.

whyPoints.title: Marked work, not impressions
whyPoints.description: Every session produces something readable with a band on it. That is the whole proposition of this page. Parents in Ajman who cannot assess a TOK argument themselves can still assess whether the band history is moving and whether the named faults are being fixed.

whyPoints.title: A specialist pool the emirate does not have locally
whyPoints.description: The IB Diploma cohort in Ajman is small, and the number of people nearby who have marked TOK against the published instrument is smaller. Remote one-to-one removes the geographic constraint, which is the honest reason online delivery suits a Diploma core subject in the northern emirates.

whyPoints.title: A stated limit on what a tutor will do
whyPoints.description: Reading, questioning, scoring and explaining are the job. Supplying prose, choosing objects or polishing a submission to completion are not, and the limit is written here rather than discovered later. This is the opposite of the finished-coursework market operating in this search space.

whyPoints.title: Scheduling that survives an Ajman week
whyPoints.description: Sessions sit after the commute, move after Iftar during Ramadan, and pause through mock fortnights and school trips without penalty. A plan that ignores the mandatory UAE subjects and a DP1 timetable is a plan that quietly stops being followed by October.

whyPoints.title: One brief across the core
whyPoints.description: TOK and the Extended Essay share a bonus point matrix and an instrument-driven marking culture. Keeping both in one record makes it possible to see which component is actually holding the total down, instead of buying hours for whichever one the student complains about.

faqs.question: What should an Ajman family receive in writing after a Theory of Knowledge session?
faqs.answer: A scored document. It should carry a band out of ten for the task discussed, the instrument's own wording quoted beside that band, margin comments naming each fault rather than describing the style, an ordered list of changes with the biggest lever first, and a date. The date is what makes a record possible: three dated drafts across a term show movement, while three pleasant conversations show nothing. If a tutor returns only corrected grammar and encouragement, you have bought proofreading rather than TOK support, and the band will not move.

faqs.question: How can I judge whether my child's TOK is improving if I have never studied it?
faqs.answer: You read the band history rather than the argument. The TOK assessment instrument has five bands, each described in a paragraph, and a competent marker will write the band and the reason on every version. Your job is to check three things: that the band is recorded each time, that the named faults from one version are actually addressed in the next, and that the student can say out loud what changed and why. None of that requires you to know what an area of knowledge is.

faqs.question: Why did my daughter's exhibition commentary score in the middle when the writing was good?
faqs.answer: Almost always because the objects describe rather than argue. The exhibition asks for three specific objects connected to one of 35 prompts, explained within 950 words in total. A commentary that tells the reader what each object is, and then asserts a link to the prompt, sits mid-band however well it reads. The repair is mechanical: for each object, state the claim it supports, then state what it fails to show. That turns description into the evaluated discussion the instrument rewards.

faqs.question: Is it worth starting Diploma core support in DP1 rather than waiting for DP2?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the reason is timetabling rather than urgency. The exhibition falls in DP1 while subject content is still relatively light, so there is room to produce, score and revise a commentary properly. By DP2 the same hours are competing with Internal Assessments and examination revision across six subjects, plus the mandatory UAE subjects. Starting in DP1 also means the student learns to band their own work early, which reduces how many paid hours the essay needs later in the programme.

faqs.question: How many objects and prompts does the TOK exhibition actually require?
faqs.answer: Three objects and one prompt. The student chooses a single prompt from the 35 internal assessment prompts published by the IB, selects three specific objects with real provenance, and explains each connection in a commentary capped at 950 words for all three together. The exhibition is marked in school against the assessment instrument and then moderated by the IB, and it contributes one third of the final TOK grade, with the externally marked essay carrying the other two thirds.

faqs.question: Can a tutor change the wording of a prescribed title to suit my son's interests?
faqs.answer: No. The six prescribed titles released for each session are used exactly as published, and an essay answering a reworded version of a title loses marks for relevance no matter how good the argument is. What a tutor can legitimately do is gloss the title: underline the command terms and the restricting words, explain in plain language what the wording excludes, and help the student decide whether a different one of the six titles fits their available examples better. That decision is cheap in week one.

faqs.question: What does a usable prescribed title plan look like on one page?
faqs.answer: Five parts. The title copied exactly, with command terms and restricting words underlined. A gloss of each key term in the student's own words. Two areas of knowledge that genuinely contrast rather than duplicate each other. One detailed, describable example for each, ideally from a subject the student studies. And a counterclaim per area carrying its own evidence rather than a single sentence of concession. A plan in that shape is markable in ten minutes, which is why it is the first artefact a session should produce.

faqs.question: My son's draft has no counterclaim worth the name. How is that fixed in one session?
faqs.answer: By giving the counterclaim equal weight rather than a sentence. A draft that concedes briefly and moves on sits below a draft that argues the opposite position with its own named example and then explains why it is less convincing. In a session the tutor identifies the paragraph where the concession sits, the student supplies a real counterexample from their own subjects, and the paragraph is rebuilt by the student afterwards. The change is usually visible as a band movement in the next dated version.

faqs.question: Does a grade E in Theory of Knowledge really stop the whole Diploma?
faqs.answer: Yes. A grade E in either TOK or the Extended Essay is a failing condition for the award of the IB Diploma, independent of how strong the six subject grades are. The two components also combine in a published matrix worth up to three bonus points on the total of 45. That is why a visible band history matters: a draft sitting in the lowest band in week eight is a fact a family can act on, whereas a vague worry in April is usually too late to fix properly.

faqs.question: If TOK and the Extended Essay are both mid-band, which one should we spend hours on?
faqs.answer: Usually TOK, because both of its tasks are short and share one instrument, so a named fault can be fixed and re-scored within a fortnight. The exception is the matrix position: if the Extended Essay is at D, lifting TOK may add nothing to the bonus points, so the hours belong to the essay instead. This is a decision you can only make with two scored records side by side, which is the argument for keeping both core components in a single brief.

faqs.question: What exactly will a tutor refuse to do with a TOK draft?
faqs.answer: Supply prose, rewrite paragraphs on the student's behalf, choose the three exhibition objects, or hand over a model answer to adapt. The submitted work has to be the student's own, and only one essay draft may be formally commented on before the final version. What a tutor does instead is read, question, score against the instrument and explain what the band language means. Any provider offering a finished essay or a completed Internal Assessment is selling the student a malpractice investigation, not a grade.

faqs.question: Can my child use an AI tool on TOK work, and will anyone be able to tell?
faqs.answer: A tool may be used as a source and must then be acknowledged properly, like any other source; text generated elsewhere presented as the student's own argument is malpractice. There is also a practical reason to avoid it in TOK specifically. Machine prose about knowledge questions is fluent, generic and reliably mid-band, because it describes positions instead of weighing them against examples the student can defend in conversation. A dated version history in the student's own voice is the better protection.

faqs.question: Can sessions move after Iftar during Ramadan, and what happens in mock fortnight?
faqs.answer: Yes to both, and the record is designed for it. During Ramadan most Ajman families shift the slot to after Iftar, which a remote tutor can accommodate without travel. In mock fortnight no new writing is attempted; the session becomes an oral defence of an existing draft, where the student argues their claims without the text in front of them. That still generates evidence, and a claim that survives questioning usually survives the examiner. Sessions pause without penalty for school trips.

faqs.question: Does the Ministry of Education or any emirate authority set what TOK my child studies in Ajman?
faqs.answer: No. TOK content and assessment are set by the IB, and the Ministry of Education supervises private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah rather than writing the Diploma syllabus. What the federal rules do require is Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies alongside the licensed curriculum, which affects how many hours a DP1 week actually contains. Internal TOK deadlines are set by each school, so an Ajman student attending a Sharjah campus follows that school's calendar.

faqs.question: Does the TOK grade matter for UAE Ministry of Education equivalency or university entry?
faqs.answer: Equivalency rules are published by the Ministry of Education and should be checked on moe.gov.ae or with the attestation authority directly, and no IB points threshold is reproduced here because that figure has not been read on an official UAE source. For the British track the published requirement is five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than grade E or 3, excluding Arabic and Islamic Education, plus one A-Level at E or two AS-Levels. Tutoring is never required for a regulatory process.

faqs.question: What happens if no TOK specialist is free when we get in touch?
faqs.answer: You are told, rather than matched with whoever is available. The pool of tutors who have marked TOK against the published instrument is genuinely small, and a general essay tutor reading a prescribed title plan is not the same service. If nobody suitable is free, the options are to wait for a named slot, start with the Extended Essay side of the core where cover is wider, or take a single scored diagnostic now so the band is at least recorded while you decide.

ajman/ib-dp-theory-of-knowledge-tutor.closingHeading: Start with one scored draft, then decide
ajman/ib-dp-theory-of-knowledge-tutor.closingBody: The cheapest useful thing an Ajman family can do about Theory of Knowledge is put the work that already exists in front of someone who marks against the instrument and ask for a band in writing. That takes one 45-minute session on Gulf Standard Time, costs nothing, and produces a document you keep whatever you decide next. If the band is secure, you have saved the money. If it is not, you know which fault caps it and in what order to fix things. Send the current commentary, title plan or draft, tell us the school's internal deadline, and we will schedule after the commute.

intro.heading: Two numbers decide what IB support costs you, and the rate is the smaller one
paragraphs: Every provider in this market advertises the first number and almost none of them discusses the second. The first is the hourly rate. The second is the number of hours, and it is the one that actually determines the cheque. A tutor at AED 150 an hour who needs thirty-two hours to repair a Higher Level problem costs AED 4,800. A tutor at AED 270 who needs twelve costs AED 3,240 and finishes sooner. Comparing rates without comparing hours is the most expensive habit a family can bring to this decision.

The second number depends on three things: whether the gap is technique or content, whether the student does the work set between sessions, and how early you start. All three are knowable before you commit, and the first can be read from a single marked script. That is why this page spends more time on plan shapes and on a calendar than on a rate card, and why the one figure we will not publish is a price for a predicted outcome.

The figures used throughout are market figures with their sources named. A 2026 Dubai tutoring cost survey puts in-home one-to-one visits at AED 180 to 350 an hour, and independent home tutors at AED 200 to 500 once travel sits inside the rate. Unitors publishes IGCSE tuition from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. TutorChase quotes AED 270 for specialist work. EdFlik advertises from AED 45 to 65 and Tutopiya from AED 33 to 52 at the budget end, which is generally group or university-student tutoring rather than specialist one-to-one. All were researched in October 2026.

Ajman changes several of those numbers in ways a generic UAE page will not tell you. The emirate is small and its private schools sit under federal Ministry of Education oversight rather than under an emirate authority. A large share of households have a parent working in Dubai or Sharjah, which pushes the usable evening later and shortens the window in which a visiting tutor can arrive. And the local pool of IB subject specialists is thin, which is the single biggest upward pressure on any in-home quote here: scarcity, not quality, sets that premium.

One thing to settle before the detail. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE; sending a teacher to a residence is a service we run only in India. The in-home option is priced honestly on this page because you will be quoted for it elsewhere and you deserve a fair comparison. What IB Gram delivers to an Ajman family is one-to-one tuition over live video, with the first lesson free and no payment taken before it. Read the bands below as a yardstick for whatever quote lands in your inbox, and convert every one of them to dirhams per teaching hour before you compare two providers.

ajman/ib-home-tutor.programmesIntro: An hour does not cost the same at every stage, because the work in the hour is different. These are the stages an Ajman family pays for, and what the money is actually buying at each one.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme, Years 7 to 11
programmes.description: The cheapest hours in the whole sequence and the ones most families skip. Work is assessed against four criteria per subject on a 1 to 8 scale, and the criterion that scores low is almost always the one asking for evaluation or reflection rather than for knowledge. Support here targets durable skills — writing to a criterion, arithmetic fluency, structured paragraphs — which is why an hour bought in Year 9 does more than an hour bought in DP2.
programmes.countryNote: In Ajman the Middle Years enquiry usually arrives in Year 10, after a report that looked fine until the student met the Diploma's expectations. At market rates the stage sits at the lower end of the qualified-tutor band published by Unitors, because the content demand on the tutor is lower even where the teaching skill required is not.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme, first year
programmes.description: The expensive year to under-spend in. Higher Level content accelerates sharply, internally assessed components open, and the core starts making demands at exactly the point the subjects do. Money spent here buys technique that applies across both years: command terms, written method, the discipline of closing an evaluative answer. Money not spent here tends to be spent twice in DP2 under time pressure.
programmes.countryNote: Ajman's IB cohorts are small, so a Higher Level group may number four or five students taught by a teacher carrying two other courses. That is the structural reason DP1 support is the most common enquiry we take from the emirate, and it is why we quote per subject rather than per student.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme, final year
programmes.description: The year when rates in this market move, because demand concentrates. Published monthly estimates for weekly one-hour specialist support in an examination year reach AED 1,000 to 2,000 and above, against AED 600 to 1,200 for mid-tier support, in the 2026 survey quoted above. Internally assessed work closes, predicted grades are set, and the remaining movable marks are mostly technique rather than content.
programmes.countryNote: The practical Ajman consequence is availability rather than price. Specialist slots between 18:30 and 21:00 — the only window that survives a Dubai or Sharjah commute — are the first to fill in the second year. Families who hold a standing slot from September pay the same as everybody else and get the hour they need.

programmes.name: The Extended Essay and Theory of Knowledge
programmes.description: Priced by most providers as a separate block, and the block that is most often bought too late. The core is assessed through an exhibition of objects, a prescribed-title essay and a supervised piece of independent research, and the failure mode is almost always sequencing rather than ability. Short blocks of process coaching, bought early, replace long blocks of crisis work bought in the final term.
programmes.countryNote: Supervision sits with the school, and a tutor's contribution is questioning the student's own work against the criteria. One operator in this market advertises finished internal assessments for a four-figure sum; that is the one line item an Ajman family should refuse at any price, because the consequence falls on the student.

ajman/ib-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: Rates vary by subject more than most price pages admit, and the reason is supply rather than difficulty. These are the subjects Ajman families most often ask about, with a note on what moves the number.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The most requested Diploma subject in this emirate and therefore the best supplied, which keeps quotes near the middle of the qualified-tutor band. Higher Level adds genuine content rather than harder versions of the same content, so hours needed rise steeply at HL even where the rate does not.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Slightly thinner supply than Analysis and Approaches, and a different cost profile: the exploration and the technology papers need a tutor comfortable with the graphic display calculator as a teaching tool rather than as an accessory, which narrows the field and lifts the quote.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Among the dearest hours in the Diploma, because two separate failure modes need two different drills and because Higher Level specialists are scarce in the northern emirates. A quote near the top of the specialist band is defensible here in a way it is not in a well-supplied subject.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Similar scarcity to Chemistry, with a mark-loss pattern that is cheap to fix once named: method written down rather than held in the head. Families often buy a long block when a short technique block would have done, which is a cost of poor diagnosis rather than of the subject.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Better supplied than the other two sciences, so quotes sit lower. The hours tend to be more numerous, because the content volume is large and the extended-response marks turn on command terms that need repeated marked practice rather than a single explanation.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Reasonably supplied and often mis-bought. The movable marks are concentrated in evaluation and in the internally assessed commentaries, both of which respond to a handful of sessions, so a year-long weekly arrangement is frequently more than the problem requires.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Quotes near the middle of the band. The cost risk here is the internally assessed component, where students choose an organisation they cannot get data from and then need far more hours than planned to rescue a question that was never answerable.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Supply is decent, and the hours are predictable because the skills are specific: unseen analysis, the individual oral's connective argument, essay structure. This is a subject where marking-only arrangements often deliver most of the movement at a fraction of the weekly cost.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Thin local supply, which lifts quotes, and a heavy load of precise terminology and studies. Families underestimate the hours because the content reads accessibly; the marks sit in command-term discipline and in the experimental study's method.

subjects.name: Arabic and the mandatory UAE subjects
subjects.description: The hardest stream to resource locally and therefore the least predictable quote. Teaching conditions are set centrally, including the language of instruction and the separation of classes for Arab and non-Arab students, so material cannot be substituted freely by a private tutor.

ajman/ib-home-tutor.regionsTitle: Ajman district by district, and what each one does to the cost of a visit
ajman/ib-home-tutor.regionsIntro: On an in-home quote, geography is money. These are the districts we hear from, with what the approach drive and the usable evening window do to the number a visiting tutor would charge.

regions.name: Al Nuaimiya
regions.note: Close to the Sharjah boundary and heavily built up, so a tutor driving from Sharjah arrives quickly but into evening congestion. The usable window starts late, which pushes visiting tutors towards a two-hour minimum to make the trip worth it.

regions.name: Al Rashidiya
regions.note: Central, with short internal journeys and reasonable access from both Sharjah and central Ajman. One of the few districts where a visiting tutor's travel element is genuinely small, and therefore where in-home quotes sit nearest the published floor.

regions.name: Al Mowaihat
regions.note: Spread-out villa district with longer internal drives. Households here commonly run two or three children, which is where the per-child economics of a visit change: one trip, several hours billed, and a single room shared by siblings.

regions.name: Al Rawda
regions.note: Established and residential, with a high share of DP1 and DP2 students. Demand concentrates in the same evening window, so this is where specialist availability rather than rate becomes the binding constraint in the final year.

regions.name: Al Jurf
regions.note: Mixed industrial and residential on the Sharjah side, with the longest approach from central Dubai. A visiting tutor pricing this district honestly is pricing forty to sixty minutes of unbilled driving into the hour.

regions.name: Al Helio
regions.note: Newer residential pockets, younger households and more Middle Years enquiries than Diploma ones. Quotes here are lower because the stage is earlier, which is exactly the stage at which the money works hardest.

regions.name: Ajman Corniche and Al Zorah
regions.note: Coastal, lower density and shorter school runs, so slightly earlier slots are workable. The in-home premium is smaller here than inland, and the enquiries skew towards Group 4 sciences at Higher Level.

schoolClusters.city: Ajman
schoolClusters.note: Private schools in the emirate sit under federal Ministry of Education oversight, and IB provision is concentrated rather than widespread. That concentration is the reason specialist tuition in the emirate is priced for scarcity. Students we support attend schools across this group.

schoolClusters.city: Sharjah, within the daily commute
schoolClusters.note: Many Ajman households drive a child across the boundary for school, and that journey is the hidden line in every in-home quote: it removes the early-evening hour in which a visiting tutor could otherwise be cheap.

ajman/ib-home-tutor.modesIntro: Three ways to buy, priced differently because they contain different amounts of the tutor's time. All three run one-to-one over live video.

modes.title: Weekly standing hour
modes.description: The highest-cost and highest-information arrangement. The tutor marks a timed task before each session, teaches inside the hour, and sets the next task, so the billed hour contains unbilled preparation. This is the shape to buy when the gap is content as well as technique, and the shape to stop paying for once the targeted criterion has moved and held for a month.
bullets: Marking done before the session, not inside it
A written note each week naming the criterion targeted
Reviewed at week six against six marked pieces
Slots after 18:30 to survive a Dubai or Sharjah commute

modes.title: Marking and feedback only
modes.description: The cheapest arrangement per unit of movement and the most demanding of the student. They sit a paper to time, send it, and the session is spent entirely on the marked script. It costs a fraction of weekly teaching because the teaching hours are the student's own, and it is a waste of money where the independent study habit does not already exist.
bullets: One script a fortnight, sat to the real time limit
Marked against the published assessment criteria
A criterion log that accumulates across the block
Early, honest warning when the work is not being done

modes.title: A short block with a deadline attached
modes.description: Four to eight hours around a specific event: an internally assessed component's school deadline, a mock week, the final technique push before papers. Blocks are the right purchase when the target is defined and the wrong purchase when it is general improvement, because an undefined block becomes a weekly arrangement by accident and nobody notices the switch.
bullets: A named target and an end date agreed up front
Criteria read together before any drafting begins

sections.heading: The in-home premium, decomposed into minutes
paragraphs: Published in-home rates in this market run from AED 180 to 350 an hour in the 2026 survey quoted above, and from AED 200 to 500 for independent home tutors, against roughly AED 150 to 300 for a qualified subject tutor working online. The gap is not a quality gap. It is a travel gap, a minimum-booking gap and a risk gap, and once you can see the three separately you can judge whether any particular quote is reasonable.

Travel comes first. A tutor who drives from Sharjah to Al Jurf and back has spent forty to sixty minutes unpaid unless it is inside the rate, which it always is. Fuel and any tolls go the same way. Then the minimum booking: because the journey is fixed and the teaching is variable, visiting tutors across the UAE price a two-hour minimum, which is why monthly in-home packages in this market appear as four two-hour sessions at AED 1,599 to 1,799 rather than as eight single hours.

Then risk. A cancelled online session costs a tutor an empty hour. A cancelled visit costs them the hour plus the journey, which is why in-home cancellation terms are tighter and why a family that moves sessions around a school calendar pays more for the privilege. None of this is unfair. It is simply what is inside the number, and a visiting tutor who quotes AED 300 for a district forty minutes away is not overcharging, they are pricing their own time correctly.

The table below sets out where the billed time in a visit actually goes. Read the last column, because that is the one that answers the only question worth asking: what does the student get for it? Two of those rows deliver something a screen cannot, and the rest deliver logistics.

sections.heading: The two Diploma years as a cash-flow calendar
paragraphs: Families budget tuition as a monthly subscription and then discover it is seasonal. The demand on a Diploma student is not spread evenly across twenty-four months: it concentrates around internally assessed deadlines, mock weeks and the final run to papers, and a plan that spends the same amount every month either over-buys in quiet terms or under-buys in the loud ones.

The useful exercise is to lay the two years out and decide in advance which months carry hours. In the first term of DP1 the right purchase is usually diagnosis plus technique, which is cheap and durable. Through the middle of DP1 the internally assessed components open and the core begins, which is where short blocks earn their keep. The first term of DP2 is the heaviest, because components close while content continues. The final stretch is technique and timed papers, and the month after the papers costs nothing at all.

The indicative monthly figures in the table come from the published 2026 estimates for weekly one-hour support: AED 240 to 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-tier and AED 1,000 to 2,000 and above for specialist examination-year support. They are the market's numbers, not a quote, and the point of the table is the shape rather than the totals.

One planning note that saves real money. No IB session or results date is published on this page, because those dates have not been confirmed from the IB's own site for this project. The school's coordinator holds the authoritative internal calendar, including component deadlines that sit months before anything external. Ask for it in September of DP1 and build the spending plan on that document rather than on a guess.

sections.heading: Who actually bears which cost in each arrangement
paragraphs: Cost incidence is the part of this market nobody writes down. Every arrangement contains the same underlying costs — travel, preparation, marking, resources, a room, cover when somebody is unavailable — and the arrangements differ in who carries each one. A quote that looks cheap often looks that way because a cost has been moved onto the family or onto the student without being named.

The clearest example is marking. A session spent reading the student's work for the first time is a session in which you paid a specialist rate for silent reading. A tutor who marks before the hour has absorbed that preparation into their rate, which makes their rate look higher and their hours fewer. Over a term the second arrangement is usually cheaper and always more useful, but you cannot see that from the two numbers on the advert.

The second example is cover. If a tutor becomes unavailable mid-block, somebody bears the cost of the gap: either the family waits, or the provider rematches and the new tutor spends a session catching up, or the marked-work record travels and the handover costs nothing much. Which of those happens is worth agreeing before the second lesson rather than in March.

The third is the room. An in-home visit uses your room, your electricity and your household's silence for two hours; an online session uses a corner of a desk. Neither is free, and for an apartment household in Al Nuaimiya the second is considerably less disruptive than the first. The table sets the comparison out in full.
